extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers / novelists wanting to use or understand unreliable narrators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for novelists on when and how to use an unreliable narrator, describing types, effects on readers, point-of-view considerations, and drafting techniques to create satisfying deception and revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable Narrator Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator can be defined as any narrator who misleads readers, either deliberately or unwittingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many are unreliable through circumstances, character flaws or psychological difficulties. In some cases, a narrator withholds key information from readers, or they may deliberately lie or misdirect. The term dates from Booth (1961) but examples exist throughout literature (e.g., Chaucer's Wife of Bath, Shakespeare's Hamlet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on readers — delight vs. betrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: If written well, the unreliable narrator will cause the reader to experience the delight of a shocking twist or a dawning realisation that they have been misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers side with the storyteller; discovering they've been double-crossed can create complex, conflicted feelings. However, if readers feel outright lied to with no way to sniff out the truth, the effect is negative. The writer must manage reader reaction carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance mistruths with foreshadowing and clues
rubrics_metrics.description: It's essential to balance the mistruths with some careful foreshadowing and stitching in of 'clues' so that when readers look back after the reveal they feel satisfied and impressed rather than frustrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreshadowing and subtle clues let readers retrospectively validate the twist. Anti-pattern: hiding everything with no trace of clue — leads to reader anger rather than delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator usually tells the story in first person, but there are notable exceptions such as limited third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider POV strategically: limited third can still be unreliable (e.g., And Then There Were None uses an unknown narrator showing multiple points of view). Using several points of view lets readers compare accounts and judge reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose check — is an unreliable narrator right for your story?
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about how your use of the technique will improve your story: would it allow you to fit an intricate plot together more effectively, showcase a complex character, or drive the story in a way a truthful narrator would not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with any device, know why you're using it. Unreliable narrators can be 'incredibly fun' but should be used to serve the story rather than as a gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type: Deliberately Unreliable Narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who lie, obscure and otherwise deliberately mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often (but not always) a 'baddie'. Even deceitful characters must be believable and have a motive for their behaviour; no one is 'just plain evil' for no reason. Example: Amy Dunne (Gone Girl) crafts a retrospective diary to frame her husband. Also note milder forms, like a narrator hiding infidelity to paint themselves in a better light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type: Impaired Narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators whose substance use (e.g., alcohol, drugs) creates holes in their story and misrememberings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alcohol is a common, widely understood device because readers can empathise with memory blanks (example: Rachel in The Girl On The Train). Drug use may function similarly but can be harder for readers to relate to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type: Psychologically Unreliable Narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators whose psychological issues or traumas have jumbled up their memories or made it hard for them to understand events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give such characters nuance and characteristics outside their 'issues' — avoid using trauma or illness merely to drive plot or mislead. Example: Patrick Bateman (American Psycho) — reality versus unreliable perception can be thrilling but must be handled responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type: Unaware Narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators who are passing on information they've been told by another unreliable character, sometimes due to blind trust or memory conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases like a protagonist with a condition that erases memories each day (example: Before I Go To Sleep) where the narrator's reports depend on others' testimony and found records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type: Naïve Narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators who lack the maturity or experience to understand the events they describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Child or youthful perspectives can simplify adult situations or misinterpret events (examples: Pi in Life of Pi; Holden Caulfield in The Catcher in the Rye). Adult-naïve narrators (Notes on a Scandal) can also misread social cues due to loneliness or skewed moral codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: Write as if the narrator is entirely honest (first draft), then revise to introduce deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the narrator as if they're entirely honest and you (the writer) completely believe the story they are telling; in revision, change some details to lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach helps create a narrator readers trust until the reveal. Example: the author describes drafting the story believing characters' accounts, then altering details later to craft the unreliable effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain truthful details to foster reader trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep as many details accurate as possible so readers truly buy into the narrator's story up until the reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrator lies frequently from the start, readers will not put stock in their story and the reveal loses impact. Build credibility through consistent, believable truthful details to maximise the twist's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple POVs or comparative narration to complicate reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling the story from several points of view allows readers to try to work out which narrators are unreliable and which are reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locked-room or ensemble narratives (Agatha Christie examples) let the reader weigh conflicting accounts; multiple unreliable narrators can create a 'twisty' reading experience but require careful management to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre suitability — often crime/thriller but broadly applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narrators feature frequently in crime and thriller books, but the technique can be used to withhold information and surprise readers of any genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include romantic suspense (The Man Who Didn't Call) and bestselling mysteries. Consider whether the device supports suspense and surprise in your particular genre.
